newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: FEATURE - Yugoslav textile industry faces collapse.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Yugoslav textile industry faces collapse.

text.p: Rump Yugoslavia's textile and leather industry, once the top export earner, faces total collapse unless the government takes urgent measures to assist its recovery.
Textile and leather exports from Serbia and Montenegro, the two republics which comprise rump Yugoslavia, were worth $1.68 billion before the breakup of the former federation in 1991.

"The ready-made garments sector alone accounted for 15 percent of total exports from former Yugoslavia, with food products next at 7.8 percent," Vera Paranos of the Yugoslav Chamber of Commerce told Reuters.
The former Yugoslav Federation, which broke up in 1991-92, also included Croatia, Slovenia, Bosnia and Macedonia, but most of the textile industry was based in Serbia.

The industry was one of the hardest hit by international sanctions imposed on rump Yugoslavia in 1992 for its involvement in the Bosnia war, mainly because it is largely dependent on imports, which immediately dried up.
DECLINE HAS CONTINUED SINCE SANCTIONS SUSPENDED

But textile industry output has continued to decline following the suspension of sanctions last November, when Serbian leader Slobodan Milosevic helped negotiated the Bosnia peace accord in Dayton, Ohio.
In the January-August 1996 period, output dropped in the yarns and fabrics sector by six percent and in the ready made garments sector by 3.4 percent against the same period last year.
Exports of the textile and leather industry together were worth just $59 million in the January-July period.
Like the rest of the Yugoslav economy, the textile industry is buckling under the burden of internal debt, lack of working capital, expensive credits, high taxes and a large workforce.
"Although the number of workers has dropped to 170,000 from 212,000 in 1991, it is still a heavy burden on an industry operating at less than 30 percent of capacity," Paranos said.
During the 42-month embargo, textile manufacturers lost most of their foreign partners, who turned to other cheap labour markets, mainly in Eastern Europe.
"If a spare part was missing, it could not be imported. It was taken off another machine, which went into scrap iron. We are now in a tragic state, terribly outdated," Paranos said.
Restoration of former ties has been slow, and most producers have been reduced to accepting low-priced deals for processing customer-supplied goods.
"Processing deals now account for 95 percent of our exports, compared to 50 percent before sanctions, but at less than half the previous price," Paranos said.
"All we are investing here is labour and energy, but at least it is keeping our capacity more or less running."
TEXTILE WORKERS AT BOTTOM OF WAGE LADDER
Compared to other sectors, textile workers are at the bottom of the wage ladder, earning an average 280 dinars ($55) in July.

"I was much better off when I was on compulsory leave and received around 130 dinars each month for not doing anything," said Marina, a worker in the Kluz garment factory. "Now I have to spend eight hours at work for 330 dinars."
She said she used to earn a lot more before from selling goods smuggled in from neighbouring countries on flea markets.
Several months ago the industry proposed that the government import basic raw materials worth around $18 million to boost export-oriented production.
"In view of the textile industry's previous export performance, the government should take closer interest in bailing it out," Paranos said.
"But none of our requests for financing, cheaper credits, lower taxes on wages or government-financed imports have been met so far."
RETURN TO WTO MOST IMPORTANT
Paranos said Yugoslavia's return to the World Trade Organization (WTO) was most important for the industry, since it would secure preferential treatment for Yugoslav goods.
"Without WTO membership, our goods are subject to the highest customs duties, which the buyers will not take upon themselves, so we pay them if we want to export," she said.

The domestic textile industry has been hit further by the "grey economy" of goods smuggled in, mainly from Turkey, that are not subject to various taxes imposed on local producers which push up the prices of their products.

Hopes of reviving the textile industry through foreign takeovers have not been fulfilled. Foreign investors have shown little interest in the sector, and there has been no talk yet of its privatisation.
"After five years of agony, we are simply exhausted. You keep going, and then one day you can just no longer keep up," Paranos said.
Without government assistance, textile factories stood no chance of surviving, she said. "Certain things just have to be done by decree."
